title: I Will Teach You to Be Rich

facts.claim: Sethi's method sets up an automatic flow: the paycheck lands in checking, then moves by itself to retirement, savings and investment accounts and to bills. Summaries frame it as systems over willpower: the decision is taken out of your hands.
facts.source: summaries; Business Insider/GOBankingRates on his routine

facts.claim: Conscious spending plan, four buckets: fixed costs, investments, savings, guilt-free spending. One summary gives roughly 50-60% of take-home for fixed costs, about 10% investments, 5-10% savings; guilt-free spending is the remainder.
Sethi's own framing: a budget looks backward, a spending plan lets you look forward. Spend extravagantly on what you love and cut costs mercilessly on what you do not.

Sethi is 'famously indifferent' to cutting daily lattes and avoids tracking every penny; he focuses on the handful (five to ten) of financial decisions that drive most results, the 'Big Wins'. Named among them: automating savings and negotiating salary.
The 85 percent solution: acting at roughly 85% quality beats doing nothing.
A 'Rich Life' defined by the reader appears in reviews and the later edition; whether the 2009 text builds a define-cost-plan-backward method could not be confirmed.

Sethi's automation walk-through (his website): 'It's not about willpower'; automation reduces the daily decisions that lead people to do nothing. Step 1 link accounts: 401(k) to checking by direct deposit; checking to Roth IRA, savings and a credit card; free bill-pay for bills that cannot go on a card. Step 2: ask companies to move bill dates to payday.

Monthly flow in his example, payday on the 1st: 401(k) portion withheld, take-home lands in checking, keep a $500 buffer at first; on the 5th automatic transfer to savings sized by the Conscious Spending Plan (typically 5-10% of income; start with $5 if you cannot yet) and to the Roth IRA (roughly 10% of take-home); on the 7th autopay of recurring bills, preferably by credit card paid in full from checking, with an email notification to review the statement first.
He cites a 401(k) study: making enrollment opt-out instead of opt-in raised contribution rates from under 40% to nearly 100%.

'The Next $100' principle: pick the top two discretionary expenses (his: eating out and going out), cut them by 25-33% over six months, redirect the cash to investing and travel; big wins come from focusing on a couple of categories rather than trimming everything a little.
Sethi's site: once bills are paid and savings and investments are automated, the money left is yours to spend; his own example is hiring a personal stylist because he enjoys dressing well.

rejected.claim: Old 1606: Sethi interviewed hundreds of people; all smart, none implemented.
Old 1606: the four-way split of ten percent investments, 'an amount' to emergency fund etc., and 'even the least disciplined get rich'.
rejected.reason: Only the 10% investing figure has loose support; the promise is unsupported.

rejected.claim: Old 1607: daily coffee cut saves $1,500 a year; Sethi calls it mathematically right but strategically wrong.
Old 1607: rent 30-40% of income, cut to 25%; car costs; 10% raise compounding over a career; coffee under one percent.
rejected.reason: Invented or unverified figures; not used.

rejected.claim: Old 1608: 'If you were rich, what would you do?' dialogue; driving without destination metaphor; 'saving is not a virtue'.
rejected.reason: Not found in the 2009 text; looks like later-edition or invented framing.
